summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults in private are legal in Côte d'Ivoire and have never been criminalised; the country's historic-era legal inheritance did not include sodomy offences, and no statute criminalising private same-sex conduct has been enacted since.

Article 360 of the Penal Code punishes a public breach of decency with three months to two years' imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 500,000 francs. Where the breach consists of an indecent act or an act contrary to nature with an individual of the same sex, the penalty rises to six months to two years' imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 300,000 francs, doubled where the act is committed against a minor or in the presence of a minor under eighteen. Under Articles 358 and 359 the age of consent is 18 for same-sex couples and 15 for different-sex couples.

Côte d'Ivoire has no legal protection against discrimination based on gender identity or sexual orientation. The government does not recognise same-sex couples, and gay and lesbian individuals and couples are not legally recognised as eligible to adopt.

Violence against LGBTQ people is documented. The US State Department's 2023 report recorded three community deaths of LGBTQI+ persons during the year and described police responses to non-state violence as sometimes slow and ineffective and often blaming the victim, while noting that authorities were handling complaints somewhat better than in previous years. A transgender man was beaten in Abobo, Abidjan, while walking with another man.

Transgender women and other feminine-presenting people assigned male at birth face especially high risk of violence because their gender expression breaches social norms. A 2015 study in Critical African Studies documented that travestis in Côte d'Ivoire face harsher stigmatisation and violence than sexual minorities whose gender presentation avoids attention, and that they had been underserved by Ivoirian rights groups that distanced themselves from them.

During the 2010-2011 post-electoral crisis, the Force Républicaines de Côte d'Ivoire beat and abused gay men and transgender persons, most of them sex workers; complaints were not filed for fear of reprisals, and fighters were more aggressive toward transvestis. In 2012 FRCI members repeatedly raided Le Club, a bar frequented by gender and sexual minorities, mainly targeting effeminate men and transvestis, forcing them into a cargo truck, sometimes forcing them to remove clothes, and demanding a significant fine under threat of being taken to bases.

Reported conversion therapy in 2023 included a transgender man attempting suicide after being forced to attend prayer camp. Many transgender people lack secure housing.

Between early September and late October 2024, 45 assault incidents against LGBTQ people were recorded in Abidjan. Social media influencers called for violence, and misinformation circulated including a hoax that the French President had asked the Ivorian President to legalise same-sex marriage. A homophobia-motivated attack occurred at a market employing gay hair stylists, after which people avoided going out during the day and meeting publicly and remained hypervigilant; wealthier people are treated with less hostility.

In 2024 President Alassane Ouattara promised to introduce a bill to Parliament to "counter the expansion" of homosexuality.

In September 2024 the National Human Rights Council called on the public to refrain from online hatred and violence toward woubis (gay men and trans women) and lelés (lesbians and trans men), stating that despite their different sexual orientation and contrary to customs and traditions, members of this community remain above all human beings and benefit from the human rights enshrined in the Ivorian Constitution and international human rights treaties. In March 2010 the Ivorian representative stated the country would begin to take measures to ensure non-discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, but would not start awareness-raising programs because it was not a current priority.

Discrimination continues in healthcare, housing and employment, with evictions and family expulsions causing school dropout, and refusal to hire or promote, or firing, if a person's status is discovered. A doctor refused service a few years before September 2011 because of a patient's sexual orientation, until protest led to care being provided. A vocal minority of Muslim and Christian leaders preach against the community. As of 2023 state authorities are slow and sometimes ineffective at managing civilian violence but may be improving in understanding and handling complaints; many people do not report to police, believing they will not be taken seriously, with reports of police not taking violence seriously and often blaming victims.

Sexual minorities, transgender and gender non-conforming people are seen as abnormal and their identities are perceived as stemming from the Global North. The only tolerance assessment quoted in the sources concerns gay people: "There is still discrimination against gay people, but generally we are moving toward relative tolerance"; the sources provide no documented statement about societal tolerance toward transgender people specifically.
tangentialFactors:
The UNDP report of December 2024, 'African Commission Resolution 275: Ten Years of Advancing LGBT+ Rights in Africa', includes a Côte d'Ivoire country overview assessing the protective legal environment, investigation and prosecution of perpetrators, access to justice, civic space, and inclusion of LGBT+ people.

A New York Times article dated October 2024 addresses the situation of LGBTQ people in Côte d'Ivoire.

The US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Côte d'Ivoire contains limited LGBT-specific content; it covers the post-electoral crisis context, including 3,000 deaths, sexual violence and displacement.

Many transgender people lack secure housing, and discrimination continues in housing and employment, with evictions and family expulsions causing school dropout and job loss on discovery.

As of 2023, many people do not report violence to police, believing they will not be taken seriously, with reports of police not taking violence seriously and often blaming victims; authorities are slow and sometimes ineffective at managing civilian violence but may be improving in understanding and handling complaints.

The National Human Rights Council's September 2024 statement is a domestic institutional protection mechanism, calling on the public to refrain from online hatred and violence toward woubis and lelés and affirming their constitutional and treaty rights.

Conversion therapy was reported in 2023, including a transgender man attempting suicide after being forced to attend prayer camp.
outOfScopeNotes:
Human Rights Watch publishes no document, case or report on the housing of transgender prisoners in Côte d'Ivoire. Where trans detainees are placed (birth sex versus identity), whether dedicated units exist, and whether solitary confinement or segregation is used are not covered in any listed publication; on the HRW country page for Côte d'Ivoire, 'LGBT Rights' appears only as a topic-facet link. This remains unresolved and not sourced.

The sources contain no documented statement about societal tolerance toward transgender people specifically; the only tolerance assessment quoted concerns gay people. Whether that assessment extends to transgender people is not sourced.

The 2024 promise by President Ouattara to introduce a bill to Parliament to "counter the expansion" of homosexuality has no sourced outcome in this inventory; whether the bill was introduced or enacted is unresolved.

The sources do not state whether Côte d'Ivoire has enacted any statutory hate-crime provision covering gender identity or sexual orientation, or whether any anti-discrimination bill covering gender identity has been tabled; this is not sourced.
